Before the Metal Is Cut

A reproducible study of a single-lug actuator bracket

Vansh Datta · Aerospace simulation notebook 01 · 16 November 2026

The engineering question is deliberately specific: can a compact 7075 aluminum bracket carry a 2 kN downward load and remain sufficiently stiff under a 500 N side load, and what does changing the root fillet actually buy?

This is a hypothetical ground-test bracket, not a drawing from Arkwin or a part approved for flight. It combines hand calculations, exact nominal CAD, an inspectable Python solid-element solver, numerical verification, mesh refinement, and a three-radius study. The code and this initial analysis were developed with coding assistance; independent reproduction in CalculiX is an explicit next step.

Evidence boundary: the saved results are actual linear-elastic Python FEA runs. No CalculiX run, bolted-joint contact analysis, physical test, fatigue life, buckling capacity, or modal result is represented as completed. A numerical gate can fail; the notebook reports its result rather than declaring every mesh converged.

Reading path: specification → hand checks → finite-element formulation → verification → results → convergence → design tradeoff → reproduction.

1. Reproduction and provenance

Extract the complete project ZIP, open this notebook in that folder, and run the cells in order. Ordinary analysis uses NumPy, SciPy, pandas, and Matplotlib. CadQuery is needed only to regenerate STEP files. The HTML version contains its figures, equations, tables, and code and can be embedded as a static page.

RUN_SOLID = False reuses the included, genuinely executed solid-model results. Set it to True to rebuild the recorded mesh series; this may take several minutes and several GB of RAM. There are no fabricated example rows. Missing cached data raise an error with instructions. The solver source and data hashes are checked.

2. Define the hardware before defining the mesh

The concept is a single central lug, captured between the two ears of a mating fork. It is not itself a two-ear clevis. A retained 12 mm pin transfers the downward load through the bore. A collar or washer transfers the axial-to-pin side load onto the web face. The mating fork, pin, collar, and four bolts are outside this model.

Coordinates are right-handed: x spans the 100 mm base length and 40 mm web width; y spans the 60 mm base width and 8 mm web thickness; z points up from the base underside. Every dimension below is nominal and in mm. No fit or machining tolerance has been assigned.

FeatureDefinition
Basex = −50…50; y = −30…30; z = 0…6
Upright webx = −20…20; y = −4…4; z = 6…66
Lug boreDiameter 12; center (0, 0, 48); axis parallel to y
Bolt clearance boresDiameter 6.6; axes parallel to z; centers (±38, ±20)
Root filletsTwo concave cylindrical blends, parallel to x, between web and base
Baseline / variantsr = 5 mm baseline; r = 2 and 10 mm variants
Nominal alloy7075-T651 plate, machined as a single piece
InterfacesFixed bolt-bore surfaces; base underside otherwise traction-free

The material is changed from the draft's generic T6 description to T651 plate to make the proposed stock form explicit. The CAD geometry has square web ends and sharp bore entrances. Those idealizations create local stress concerns and are not an instruction to machine unbroken edges.

Chosen study targets, not externally supplied requirements: mass below 160 g; load-weighted displacement below 0.05 mm for the 2 kN downward case and below 0.15 mm for the 500 N side case. These targets create a useful stiffness tradeoff. They do not demonstrate compatibility with a real actuator.

3. Material inputs and the meaning of a margin

Kaiser's 7075 plate technical data lists typical T651 tensile yield and ultimate strengths of 503 and 572 MPa, ultimate shear strength of 331 MPa, and elastic modulus of 71 GPa. This notebook uses those typical values for educational screening. Poisson ratio 0.33 and density 2810 kg/m³ are declared modeling assumptions.

These are not thickness-, orientation-, and procurement-specific design allowables. The final choice of plate and the material certificate could change the strength inputs. We do not equate tensile yield strength to bearing strength, and we do not turn a typical fatigue value into a life prediction.

For a specified stress quantity and an applicable allowable, the margin is

A positive number is meaningful only if both terms represent the same failure mode. Comparing a local von Mises stress with tensile yield is an elastic yield screen. It is not a lug bearing allowable, a bolt check, or proof of ultimate load capacity. The 1.5 factor is selected for this exercise, not claimed as compliance with a particular regulation.

4. Hand calculations: follow the load path

Downward case: the pin pushes on the lower half of the bore; load travels down the web, through the filleted root and flexible base, and into the four constrained bores. Nominal bearing stress is force divided by projected bearing area:

The straight web below the hole carries gross compressive stress approximately P/(bt). A hypothetical upward/reversed load would instead make the top ligament, net-section tension, and tear-out screens relevant. For that separate screening direction, the top-edge center distance is e = 18 mm:

Those two formulas are not a tensile failure assessment of the current downward case. A true reverse-load FEA must move the bearing pressure onto the upper half of the bore; simply negating the existing contact-pressure traction is unphysical.

For a 12 mm pin supported by the mating fork in ideal double shear:

This excludes pin bending, clearance, nonuniform bearing, and pin material selection.

5. Why the smaller load is more demanding

The side load bends the web about its thin direction. Treating it as a rectangular cantilever with height H = 42 mm gives

The thickness is cubed in the stiffness. A modest change in thickness can matter more than a large increase in tensile strength. A fillet can reduce local stress and stiffen the root, but it does not turn the web into a different alloy.

For comparison, straight-web shortening under the downward load is

These are deliberately reduced models. They omit the hole, collar footprint, fillet, base bending, and elastic support compliance. Expect the solid model to differ. They test scale and load-path interpretation, not exact equality.

6. Loads and constraints in the solid model

LC1: downward limit, 2,000 N. Let the outward radial direction from the hole center into the lug material be e_r, with z component e_rz. A cosine bearing traction acts only on the lower half of the bore:

The analytical normalization above applies to the exact cylindrical surface. The implementation integrates on faceted faces and normalizes the assembled nodal loads to exactly −2,000 N in z. It also records the small quadrature-induced off-axis moments instead of silently assuming perfect symmetry.

LC2: side limit, 500 N in +y. A smooth annular pressure acts on the y = −4 mm face, centered on the hole. Its radial weighting is sin²[π(R−6)/6] for 6 < R < 12 mm and zero elsewhere, normalized to a total of 500 N. This represents a retained pin collar spreading thrust onto the face. It is a prescribed traction surrogate, not a solved washer contact pressure.

LC3: downward factored, 3,000 N. In this small-displacement, linear-elastic model the displacement and stress fields scale exactly by 1.5, and strain energy by 2.25. LC3 is calculated by scaling LC1; it is not falsely presented as a separate nonlinear ultimate-strength simulation.

All displacement components on the four bolt-bore surfaces are fixed. The base underside is free. This is a deliberately stiff, idealized support model, not a faithful substitute for bolts, preload, contact, friction, or a mating plate. Support-edge peaks can be singular. The scenarios are separate, not simultaneous; a combined loading assessment is part of the agent handoff.

7. An inspectable finite-element formulation

The governing equations are small-strain isotropic elasticity with no body force:

The weak form leads to element stiffness and the assembled linear system:

The code uses ten-node tetrahedra with quadratic Lagrange displacement fields:

Geometry is affine within each tetrahedron: curved bores and fillets are represented by flat faces, and midside nodes lie at edge midpoints. Thus geometry error decreases with refinement along with displacement error. This is not a curved isoparametric mesh. Four tetrahedral integration points exactly integrate the quadratic stiffness integrand for homogeneous material on affine elements. Seven-point, degree-five triangle quadrature integrates applied surface loads.

The sparse system is solved with diagonally preconditioned conjugate gradients. Engineering shear strain is used in the strain vector. Stresses are unaveraged; the plotted whole-part field uses element-centroid stress, while the fillet measurement evaluates stress at boundary-face centroids in a defined region.

The source below is included for inspection. solid_fem.py is the executable version; do not edit the displayed copy without also updating the source file and rerunning the study. This custom solver is a learning tool, which makes independent verification and the later CalculiX comparison especially important.

Python · cell 5
# Inspect the implementation used for the recorded results.
import inspect, solid_fem
print(inspect.getsource(solid_fem.constitutive))
print(inspect.getsource(solid_fem.strain_matrix))
print(inspect.getsource(solid_fem.assemble))

def constitutive(E,nu):
    lam=E*nu/((1+nu)*(1-2*nu));mu=E/(2*(1+nu))
    C=np.zeros((6,6));C[:3,:3]=lam;np.fill_diagonal(C[:3,:3],lam+2*mu)
    C[3:,3:]=np.eye(3)*mu
    return C

def strain_matrix(grad,L):
    L=np.broadcast_to(L,(len(grad),4))
    dn=np.empty((len(grad),10,3)); dn[:,:4]=(4*L[:,:,None]-1)*grad
    for k,(i,j) in enumerate(EDGES):dn[:,4+k]=4*(L[:,i,None]*grad[:,j]+L[:,j,None]*grad[:,i])
    B=np.zeros((len(grad),6,30))
    B[:,0,0::3]=dn[:,:,0];B[:,1,1::3]=dn[:,:,1];B[:,2,2::3]=dn[:,:,2]
    B[:,3,0::3]=dn[:,:,1];B[:,3,1::3]=dn[:,:,0]
    B[:,4,1::3]=dn[:,:,2];B[:,4,2::3]=dn[:,:,1]
    B[:,5,0::3]=dn[:,:,2];B[:,5,2::3]=dn[:,:,0]
    return B

def assemble(p,t,E=71000.,nu=.33):
    grad,vol=gradients(p,t);C=constitutive(E,nu)
    dofs=(3*t[:,:,None]+np.arange(3)).reshape(-1,30)
    vals=np.empty((len(t),900))
    for start in range(0,len(t),512):
        sl=slice(start,start+512);ke=np.zeros((len(t[sl]),30,30))
        for L in GAUSS:
            B=strain_matrix(grad[sl],L)
            ke+=np.matmul(B.transpose(0,2,1),np.matmul(C,B))*(vol[sl]/4)[:,None,None]
        vals[sl]=ke.reshape(-1,900)
    rows=np.repeat(dofs,30,axis=1).ravel();cols=np.tile(dofs,(1,30)).ravel()
    K=coo_matrix((vals.ravel(),(rows,cols)),shape=(3*len(p),3*len(p))).tocsr()
    K.eliminate_zeros()
    return K,grad,vol,dofs,C

8. Verification before interpreting the bracket

The independent beam benchmark is a rectangular cantilever: L = 200 mm, width = 20 mm, thickness = 10 mm, E = 71,000 MPa, ν = 0.33, and a uniformly distributed 100 N transverse force on its end face. Its Euler–Bernoulli reference is

The measured FE output is the end-face force-weighted displacement. Full 3D clamping and Poisson effects differ from the beam theory assumptions, so this is an approximate benchmark, not an exact continuum solution. The acceptance band is 2% for this starter check. A closer study would refine the beam itself and compare away from its clamped boundary.

Three additional checks exercise different failure modes in the implementation: the element must reproduce a constant strain, all six rigid motions must have negligible elastic energy, and an affine displacement prescribed on the entire boundary must be recovered by solving for the interior nodes. Force balance, moment balance, energy, and free-DOF residuals are checked on every bracket solve.

9. Quantities of interest: define them before seeing the contours

The displacement measure is work-conjugate to the applied load distribution:

It is the generalized displacement under the chosen distributed loading, not a node selected after looking at the result. LC1 includes small radial displacements weighted by the radial bearing traction. LC2 is a pressure-weighted y displacement on the collar. Maximum nodal displacement is reported separately; the two quantities do not necessarily occur at the same location.

The fillet metric is the maximum unaveraged von Mises stress at boundary triangle centroids on both root fillets, within |x| < 6 mm, excluding their end edges. The area-weighted mean over that patch is also recorded. This removes sharp fillet terminations from the selected metric, but does not establish a part-wide maximum stress or prove that all local singularities are absent. The centroid-based peak is a sampled quantity whose sampling changes with mesh density.

11. Mesh refinement: a displacement can settle before the stress does

The baseline uses requested bulk spacings of 6, 4.5, 3, and 2 mm. Local feature breaks override that spacing: each fillet gets at least three angular subdivisions, and progressively more as h falls. Exact element counts are reported. Circular holes and fillets are faceted, so this is combined geometry and discretization refinement rather than pure polynomial error isolation.

For each quantity q, the relative change between adjacent refinements is

The predeclared gate is less than 2% change in both generalized displacement and the selected fillet stress, separately for each load case. This is an engineering stability check, not an estimated bound on the true error. The refinement ratio is not uniform, and stress sampling changes, so no Richardson extrapolation or Grid Convergence Index is claimed.

12. The fillet is a design variable, not a cosmetic feature

The radius comparison keeps all other nominal dimensions and load definitions fixed. Each of r = 2, 5, and 10 mm has h = 3 and 2 mm runs. Compare mass from the exact analytical geometry with response from the finest recorded mesh. The two variant meshes are a sensitivity check, not an automatic claim of converged peak stress for every geometry.

A larger radius changes both the stress flow and the effective root restraint. Therefore its effect on stiffness should be measured, not inferred solely from a stress-concentration chart. It also adds material and requires more machining clearance near the mounting interfaces.

13. What the results support—and what they do not

The result supports a statement about this modeled load path: the sideways load is more compliant because it excites bending of the thin web and its flexible base. The straight-web hand model underestimates the complete-bracket side deflection because it omits important sources of compliance. Agreement in trend is useful; exact agreement was never the right test here.

The 10 mm radius is a candidate for the next independent model, not a selected flight design. Its response must be assessed alongside convergence status, support assumptions, clearance around fasteners, and manufacturing constraints.

This table is only a typical-property local yield screen, using the selected fillet stress. It deliberately does not claim a part-wide factor of safety. It excludes bearing, pin bending, bolt strength, preload loss, fatigue, buckling, and fracture. If a mesh gate fails, the stress-derived number remains preliminary.

14. Handoff to a production solver and a physical experiment

  1. Open the three STEP files in FreeCAD and inspect dimensions, solid validity, bore axes, exact volume, and accessibility around the 10 mm fillet.
  2. Generate independent Gmsh meshes with curved quadratic geometry where valid, then solve the same loads and constraints with CalculiX C3D10 elements.
  3. Match the load resultants, their moments, and the output definitions before comparing solver results. Mesh a fillet region explicitly; do not compare one program's averaged nodal peak with the other's unaveraged centroid stress.
  4. Refine any quantity that misses the 2% gate. Compare surface sampling methods and check geometric approximation separately from displacement order.
  5. Replace the idealized support with a justified bolt/fixture/contact model. Assess the collar load spread, load reversal, and any simultaneous loads.
  6. Only then add modal analysis, a specified fatigue spectrum, or buckling as separate studies. Eigenvalue buckling alone is not a collapse prediction.
  7. A small physical test could measure displacement at a marked location under a calibrated force. Model that exact fixture and sensor location before calling it experimental validation. The generalized displacement above is not directly a dial-indicator reading.

Agent_Handoff.md contains the complete CAD, solver, and site-integration task. The current deliverable is an executed computational baseline with its remaining checks exposed, not a claim that all twelve weeks have already been completed.

15. References and further reading

  • Kaiser Aluminum: 7075 sheet, coil, and plate technical data. Typical material values only; no procurement-specific allowable inferred.
  • DefElement: degree-two Lagrange tetrahedron. Basis definition used to check the interpolation.
  • SciPy: conjugate-gradient solver. Solver interface and convergence semantics.
  • Gmsh reference manual. Independent meshing workflow planned for the local reproduction.
  • NASA NPARC: verification and validation tutorial. Distinguishing numerical verification from comparison with physical observations.
  • CalculiX official project. Planned independent solid solver; not the source of the recorded results in this notebook.
